summary:
We have developed a web-based health monitoring platform for astronauts, that track the health of the crew member that are brain, eyes, bone, muscles, kidneys, heart and mental health additionally. A comprehensive logging page where crew members fill out factor(nutrients) they had consumed with an Armstrong-8 table-based hydration check for crew members. A data visualization page each factor logged gets his own graph with space and earth based average and 1 SD range. It has comprehensive statistical model that can track the cause of a symptoms that an astronauts might face, also equipped with two CNN models for identification of calcium in urine and papilledema, every organ has its own unique weighted set of drivers (nutrients that are important to that organ), and environmental penalties are subtracted and health ring per organ shows how much health is left across the mission.
Spaceflight affects the body in ways that are slow and hard to notice, such as bone loss, muscle loss, fluid shifts, kidney-stone and isolation. Crew Health makes these visible daily and explains the cause behind the problem that crew might be facing or identify problems in advance so precautionary measure can be taken earlier, which might turn life threatening like kidney stone or excess fluid pressure in skull.

Crews on long missions need to catch small declines early and act on them. The app can support preventive care on future missions to the Moon and Mars, and it can also help people on Earth.
details:
1. What does it do and how does it work?

In one line: Crew Health is an offline early-warning system for astronauts. It turns the daily log a crew member already keeps into organ-level health scores, plain-language explanations and alerts.

Step 1: Log (one page, 35 factors).

  • Each day the crew member records:
    • Food and exercise: nutrients (calories, macros, vitamins, minerals), sleep and exercise.
    • Hydration: water intake and a one-tap Armstrong 8-colour urine chart.
    • Vitals and mind: SpO₂, mood and social-contact minutes.
    • Space environment: radiation dose, cabin CO₂ and cabin noise.
    • Symptoms: typed or tapped.
  • An empty box means “unknown”, and the grey placeholder shows the person’s own benchmark.

Step 2: Learn your normal.

  • Every factor is compared with a benchmark (age- and sex-aware RDA, or a typical space average) and with the person’s own history.
    • a green Earth band (±1 SD);
    • a blue space band after 30 space days;
    • red, orange and green dots for low days.
  • After 60 space days the baseline switches from Earth to space. Older days are down-weighted over time, because “normal” drifts as the body adapts.

Step 3: Score seven organs.

  • Brain, eyes, bone, muscles, kidneys, heart and (in space mode) mental health each earn up to 1 point a day from weighted drivers.
    • Examples: omega-3, magnesium, sleep and B12 for the brain; calcium, vitamins D and K and loading exercise for bone; protein and exercise for muscle; water and urine colour for the kidneys.
  • Daily penalties for cabin noise, CO₂ and radiation are subtracted, so a day can score anywhere from 1 to −1.
  • The ring shows the share of the planned mission earned, and each card names the top causes holding that organ back.

Step 4: Explain symptoms.

  • The user picks a symptom and the app ranks which factors in their own data are most linked to it.
  • It uses a Bayesian odds ratio plus an adjusted logistic regression (Laplace approximation) with priors from a medical knowledge base.
  • Exposure ends the day before the symptom (a one-day lag), and overlapping windows are corrected.
  • With too little data it reports a wide risk range and “Not enough data” instead of guessing.

Step 5: Alert.

  • Fixed medical rules raise the alerts: bone loss, kidney stones, radiation, CO₂ and a SANS watch after repeated vision-change days.
  • Red-flag symptoms, such as sudden vision change or possible radiation sickness, tell the crew member to contact the flight surgeon.
  • Rules decide when to warn, and statistics only explain why.

The Armstrong urine test.

  • The 8 colours map to four dehydration bands: 1–2 well hydrated (±1% body mass), 3–4 minimal (1–3%), 5–6 significant (3–5%), 7–8 serious (>5%, seek medical help).
  • The app shows a green, info, yellow or red hydration alert and a water target of body weight × band loss. For example, 70.6 kg at colour 5 is about 2.8 L.
  • Hydration also feeds the kidney bar, which links to the stone risk.

Two AI image screens (run locally, spaceflight mode).

  • Eye:
    • Model: a ConvNeXt-Tiny 5-fold ensemble reads retinal photos for papilledema, the swollen optic nerve behind SANS.
    • Training: fine-tuned from ImageNet on 1,369 fundus photos (779 normal, 295 papilledema, 295 pseudopapilledema, the harmless look-alike, treated as negative) plus augmented copies.
    • Techniques: weighted BCE loss, label smoothing, EMA weights and flip test-time augmentation.
    • Decision rule: the threshold is tuned for at least 90% sensitivity.
    • Evaluation: grouped splits keep augmented copies out of the test set, with a 15% untouched test set and 95% confidence intervals.
    • Model: a ResNet-18 multi-label classifier reads urine-sediment images.
    • Training: fine-tuned from ImageNet at 320×320 for 15 epochs (AdamW, OneCycle).
    • Output: six findings (casts, crystals, epithelial cells, red cells, white cells, yeast), scored by macro-AUROC.
    • Stone alert: the crystals label drives the stone alert.
  • Each run is saved in a monthly test history.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Earlier warning: it watches the main long-duration risks (bone and muscle loss, kidney stones, SANS, radiation, cabin air and mood) continuously, rather than only at medical check-ins.
  • Works without ground contact: everything runs on one machine, so it works when the link to Earth is slow or unavailable.
  • Personal: the baseline comes from the person’s own data, not only Earth averages.
  • Trustworthy: it shows uncertainty, keeps alerts rule-based and auditable, and sends red flags to a human.
  • Low effort and readable: the crew logs on one page and reads plain-language results, organ rings and charts. No statistician is needed.
  • Explains why: each organ names what is holding it back, and the stone chain is spelled out (microgravity, bone calcium released, kidneys filter the excess, stones can form).

3. What is the intended impact?

  • Near term: help a crew member see problems early and arrive at conversations with their flight surgeon with data instead of impressions.
  • Longer term: support crew autonomy on Moon and Mars missions, where a real-time clinic call isn’t possible.
  • Educational: show how space physiology becomes measurable inputs, scores and rules, in a form students and the public can follow.
  • Possible spill-over (not tested): hydration, nutrition and sleep monitoring for other isolated settings on Earth.

4. Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Backend: one Node.js file (Node 18 or newer, about 1,400 lines) with one SQLite database. It uses better-sqlite3, or Node’s built-in node:sqlite as a fallback.
  • Frontend: React (JSX) in the browser, with no build step, plus HTML and CSS and the Plus Jakarta Sans font.
  • AI: Python with PyTorch/torchvision to fine-tune ConvNeXt-Tiny (eye) and ResNet-18 (kidney). The datasets came from Roboflow exports.
    • NASA-STD-3001 Vol. 1 sets the 600 mSv career radiation limit. The same standard’s tables give the blood-forming-organ limits of 250 mGy-Eq (30 days) and 500 mGy-Eq (1 year): https://standards.nasa.gov/sites/default/files/standards/NASA/C//nasa-std-3001-vol-1-rev-c-signature.pdf nasa
    • NASA-STD-3001 Vol. 2 limits the average one-hour CO₂ pressure to 3 mmHg. This is explained in NASA’s CO₂ brief: https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/ochmo-tb-004-carbon-dioxide.pdf nasa
    • On SANS, the leading hypothesis is a headward fluid shift with possibly mild, chronic raised pressure in the skull. See https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7545196 nih

5. How is it creative?

  • Organ health bars: a game-like score grounded in physiology, with each organ’s drivers and penalties shown openly.
  • A baseline that adapts: “normal” shifts from Earth to space instead of being compared with fixed Earth values.
  • Honest statistics: the app says “not enough data” rather than inventing a cause, and a rule-versus-statistics split keeps alerts accountable.
  • Armstrong test as a clinical signal: a one-tap urine-colour check becomes a dehydration band, a water target, a kidney-score input and a stone-risk link.
  • Cheap images as screening tools: retinal photos for SANS and urine images for stone risk, instead of heavy hardware.
  • Offline and tiny: the whole system is one file plus one database, with no cloud and no build step.
  • Explain-first design: a plain-language line paired with a technical line everywhere, so both a crew member and a flight surgeon can read it.

6. What factors did we consider?

  • Autonomy and communication delay: offline operation and local AI.
    • Red flags escalate to the flight surgeon.
    • Uncertainty is shown, and the image threshold favours sensitivity (at least 90%) to limit missed cases.
    • The app is labelled an educational prototype, not a medical device.
    • Empty means unknown.
    • A day with under 50% of its driver weight logged earns 0 but still counts as a day.
    • Bayesian priors, a lag and overlap correction guard against false links.
  • Adaptation: the body changes in space, so the baseline switches after 60 space days and old days are down-weighted.
    • Reference values are placeholders for flight-surgeon review.
    • Symptom links are statistical associations, not diagnoses.
    • The image models are not clinically validated.
    • SANS causation is still debated, so we describe the pressure explanation as the leading hypothesis.
    • The app compares daily effective dose in mSv with organ limits that NASA states in mGy-Eq, which is a simplification.
